region_name: A sugarcane and paddy farmer in Mandya (Old Mysuru region)
region_definition: Puttaswamy is a composite portrait of a smallholder cultivator in Mandya district's Cauvery-irrigated core, drawn from documented patterns of land, caste and agrarian distress in the Old Mysuru region rather than from any single real person. He is 44 years old and farms roughly 2.5 acres of KRS-canal-fed land in Malavalli taluk, growing sugarcane and paddy in rotation, supplemented by two milch cows sold through a Nandini-affiliated dairy cooperative. He belongs to the Vokkaliga community, which Census-based and political-analysis sources describe as numerically dominant across Mandya, Ramanagara, Mysuru and rural Bengaluru. He lives with his wife Rathnamma, his elderly parents, a sixteen-year-old daughter in the tenth standard, and a thirteen-year-old son in the eighth standard, in a joint household whose annual cash income, after diesel, fertiliser and labour costs, rarely exceeds roughly one and a half lakh rupees, most of it earned once or twice a year at cane harvest and paddy sale. This profile is an analytic composite built from Census, UDISE+ and district-reporting evidence about Mandya, not a record of an identifiable individual.

daily_life_and_work.definition: This person's occupation, income, workday, and economic pressures.
daily_life_and_work.regional_profile:
Puttaswamy's work is organised around two intersecting calendars: the release schedule of Krishna Raja Sagara (KRS) canal water that irrigates his fields, and the 12-to-18-month growth cycle of sugarcane. He rises before 5 a.m. to walk his two cows to graze and to check the inlet channel watering his paddy nursery, then spends the morning in the field with his wife Rathnamma, who does most of the transplanting and weeding while he manages irrigation turns and pesticide application. Mandya district, still widely described as Karnataka's sugar bowl, is the district where sugar factories traditionally announce cane prices first, with other mills across the state following suit. But the announced price is only the start of a long negotiation, because mills routinely delay payment for cane already crushed, leaving farmers carrying arrears through the following season; district administrations have periodically had to order sugar factories to release pending price and subsidy amounts owed to farmers for a completed crushing season, with the state and mills each contributing a share per tonne meant to top up the cane price. Puttaswamy has waited out such delays more than once, borrowing first from a cooperative credit society and, when that ceiling is reached, from a private moneylender at higher interest to cover fertiliser and school costs while the mill payment is pending.

During the harvesting season, which runs roughly from December to March, Puttaswamy also works as an informal contractor for cane-cutting labour, arranging migrant gangs for his own and neighbouring farms. In the lean months between paddy transplantation and cane harvest, he and Rathnamma rely on the fortnightly milk cheque from the dairy cooperative, the household's only predictable income; in at least two bad seasons he has also taken up MGNREGA work on village road and canal-desilting projects to bridge a cash shortfall. Diesel-pump irrigation, since electricity to agricultural feeders is intermittent, is a recurring cost he cannot avoid even when the KRS reservoir is full, and a poor monsoon or an unfavourable Cauvery Water Management Authority release order to Tamil Nadu can cut his second paddy crop altogether, a risk that shapes nearly every financial decision he makes in a given year.

On roughly a third of an acre too far from the canal head to get a reliable water turn, he grows ragi and fodder grass instead of paddy, a hedge against a season when canal releases run short. In a good year, after clearing input costs and cooperative loan instalments, the household is left with perhaps one and a half lakh rupees in cash plus grain and jaggery for home use; in a year of delayed cane payment or a weak monsoon that margin disappears, and the family draws down savings meant for his daughter's college fees or his son's school supplies. He does not consider his household as poor as the tribal households in Chamarajanagara he reads about, but describes the work as one bad season away from serious debt, a description he has heard echoed by fellow farmers at the cane-price protests he periodically joins outside the mill gates.

family_and_household.definition: Household structure, marriage, children, caregiving and gender roles.
family_and_household.regional_profile:
Puttaswamy's household is a three-generation joint family: he and Rathnamma, his parents (his father can no longer work the fields but still supervises irrigation timing from the field bund), and their two children. Vokkaliga households in the Cauvery basin are documented as predominantly agrarian and rural, with land passed down through sons, and Puttaswamy's own 2.5 acres are already half of what his father once farmed before it was divided between him and his elder brother, who lives in the adjoining house and shares the diesel pump. Rathnamma's day begins earlier than his: she milks the cows, cooks for six people, transplants and weeds alongside him for several hours, and manages the kitchen garden and poultry that supplement the family's diet, a pattern of combined agricultural and domestic labour that district-level demographic accounts of rural Mandya describe as typical for women married into cultivating families, without implying it is universal or equally chosen by all households.

Decisions about the children's education and the daughter's eventual marriage are discussed jointly by Puttaswamy, his father and his brother, reflecting the extended family's continued authority over major household choices even though Rathnamma manages day-to-day domestic and dairy income. The family has not yet fixed a marriage for their daughter Chaitra, but relatives have begun making informal enquiries, a pattern district-level accounts of the Cauvery belt describe as more common once a girl completes secondary school than while she remains enrolled, without dating it to any fixed age. Their son Kiran, as the presumptive inheritor of the family's land once it is his turn to divide it with any future siblings, is already expected to learn cane and paddy cultivation directly from his father and grandfather during school holidays and the harvest season, an apprenticeship that competes directly with his schoolwork.

Caregiving for Puttaswamy's ageing parents falls almost entirely on Rathnamma, since public elder-care or nursing support does not reach a village of this size, and the family has never seriously discussed a nuclear household arrangement, both for cultural reasons and because splitting the small holding further would leave neither son with a genuinely viable farm. Property, including the house itself, remains registered jointly in the name of Puttaswamy's father, a common arrangement in the district that keeps ultimate authority over major decisions, including any future land sale, with the senior generation rather than with Puttaswamy or Rathnamma directly. Rathnamma also manages the household's small cash reserve from milk sales and vegetable-garden produce, a fund she controls more directly than farm income, which passes first through Puttaswamy and his father, and which she draws on for the children's everyday school expenses, illustrating a division of financial authority common in Cauvery-belt farming households where women often manage smaller, steadier income streams while men control the larger, seasonal cash from the main crop.

education_and_schooling.definition: This person's own schooling and their children's schooling, including real, regionally-documented reasons children like theirs might leave school before completing secondary education.
education_and_schooling.regional_profile:
Puttaswamy studied only up to the seventh standard in the village government school before his father needed him full-time in the fields, a trajectory he does not regret but does not want repeated for his own children. Chaitra, his daughter, completed government Kannada-medium schooling through the tenth standard in the village and has just cleared her SSLC exams; whether she continues to a pre-university college in Malavalli town, about ten kilometres away, depends heavily on transport and safety, since the family will not send her by shared auto or cycle on the highway. The free bus travel Karnataka's Shakti scheme has extended to all women and girls since June 2023 has changed this calculation directly: in its first year the scheme recorded over 225 crore free rides by women statewide, saving beneficiaries a combined 5,481 crore rupees in fares, at an average daily ridership of 18.1 lakh women between June 2023 and March 2024. Puttaswamy now treats a free, subsidised KSRTC bus service to the taluk town as the deciding factor in letting Chaitra pursue PU college rather than stopping her education at SSLC.

His son Kiran's risk of leaving school runs in a different direction. During the cane-harvesting season from December to March, when labour is short and cane-cutting wages rise, neighbouring families with landless or very small holdings routinely pull sons of Kiran's age out of school for weeks at a stretch to work in cutting gangs, or take them along when the family migrates for hired cane-cutting labour elsewhere in Mandya's Malavalli and Maddur taluks, a pattern documented as a recurring cause of secondary-school absenteeism in this part of the district. Puttaswamy's own landholding is just large enough that he has so far kept Kiran in school through the harvest by hiring outside labour instead, but he is aware that a bad cane-payment year could force him to use his son's labour instead of paying wages he cannot yet collect from the mill.

Karnataka's secondary-level dropout rate was recorded at 22.09% for classes 9 and 10 in UDISE+ 2023-24 data, against a 14.1% national average, and more recent UDISE+ figures put the dropout rate among girls in classes 9 and 10 at 13.9%, still above the 8% national average. Mandya district's own numbers are older but illustrative: a district survey conducted in 2013-14 recorded 2,151 out-of-school children aged 6 to 14 in the district, of whom 1,297 were boys and 854 were girls, a reminder that in this Cauvery-belt district boys' dropout linked to farm and cane labour has historically run higher than girls', the reverse of the more recent state-wide gendered pattern. Puttaswamy also worries about the growing gap between the Kannada-medium government schooling his children have received and the English-medium private schooling increasingly demanded by jobs in Bengaluru's economy; relatives working in the city have told him that Kannada-medium graduates from villages like his struggle even for entry-level private-sector jobs. For now, his strategy is to keep both children in school as long as the farm's cash flow allows, treating any dropout as a last resort forced by debt or labour shortage rather than a preference.

health_and_wellbeing.definition: Health access, risks and concerns for this person and their family.
health_and_wellbeing.regional_profile:
For ordinary illness, Puttaswamy's family relies on the primary health centre serving his village cluster, staffed by a doctor who visits on fixed days, and travels to the district hospital in Mandya town or, for anything requiring surgery or specialist care, to Mysuru's referral hospitals when the family can afford the trip and the lost farm labour it costs. The mental strain of debt and price uncertainty is not abstract to him: national human-rights authorities have investigated cane-payment delays in Mandya as a contributing factor in farmer suicides in the district, treating the issue seriously enough to seek explanations from the state government. Partly in response to this kind of agrarian distress, NIMHANS in Bengaluru piloted a telemedicine-based Primary Care Psychiatry Programme with a pilot experience in Mandya district, training local doctors to recognise and treat depression and anxiety in primary care rather than requiring a trip to a psychiatric specialist in the city; the programme later evolved into a year-long diploma course offered more widely. Puttaswamy has never personally visited a counsellor, but a cousin who did described it as the first time anyone in a government clinic had asked him directly about the stress of unpaid cane bills.

Physically, the greatest risks in his working life come from the cane and paddy fields themselves: cuts from sickles during harvest, prolonged exposure to pesticide spray without reliable protective equipment, and the strain of standing in flooded paddy fields for hours, which he and other farmers in the area associate with joint pain in later years, though he has not sought a formal diagnosis for it. Rathnamma's health is the family's lowest priority in practice, even though her working day is longer than his: she attends the primary health centre only when a condition becomes disruptive to her work, a pattern rural health researchers have linked more broadly to the low priority routinely given to women's health within agricultural households in this region. Neither Puttaswamy nor Rathnamma has health insurance beyond the state's public hospital entitlements, and a serious hospitalisation for either of them, or for his elderly parents, is the single financial risk he says worries him more than a bad monsoon.

community_and_belief.definition: Community, caste/religious context, social ties and local institutions in this person's life.
community_and_belief.regional_profile:
Puttaswamy identifies as Vokkaliga, a community Census-based and political-analysis sources describe as numerically dominant across Mandya, Ramanagara, Mysuru and rural Bengaluru, historically associated with landholding and cultivation in the Cauvery belt, though such descriptions are demographic generalisations about a large and internally diverse community rather than a claim that every Vokkaliga household farms or holds land. His family's most significant pilgrimage is to the Cheluvanarayana Swamy temple at Melukote for the Vairamudi festival, an occasion regional cultural accounts describe as a major Vokkaliga pilgrimage event in Mandya district, which Puttaswamy's family has attended most years since his childhood. The Adichunchanagiri Mutt, based in Nagamangala, functions in his understanding less as a place of worship than as an institution running schools and hostels drawing Vokkaliga students from villages like his own, and he has considered it as an option for Kiran's secondary schooling if the household's finances tighten further.

Labour on his farm during peak transplantation and harvest periods is not confined to family members: he hires day labourers from Scheduled Caste communities in his village, most often people identifying as Holeya, one of the Scheduled Caste communities the Census records as present across all six Old Mysuru districts, generally in a wage-labour rather than landowning relationship to farmers like himself, a structural pattern regional social-science literature describes without treating it as fixed or unchangeable. Puttaswamy's own social world outside the immediate family runs mainly through the village's farmers' cooperative society, informal caste-based mutual-aid networks that help arrange loans and marriages, and seasonal festivals tied to the sowing and harvest calendar, including local village-deity festivals that double as occasions for settling small community disputes. He is aware, mostly through television and conversations at the mill gate, of the ongoing political demand by Vokkaliga organisations for a larger quota under the state's backward-classes reservation framework, and supports it, though he describes the everyday texture of his community life as shaped far more by land, water and the cooperative society than by reservation politics. Religious life in the household follows the mainstream Hindu, Shaiva-Vaishnava mixed calendar common in Vokkaliga farming families of the district, combining household worship of family deities with periodic visits to larger temples such as Chamundeshwari Temple on Chamundi Hills in Mysuru during Dasara, an occasion Puttaswamy treats as both devotional and a rare family outing away from the farm.

civic_life_and_government.definition: This person's dealings with government schemes, local bodies, and politics.
civic_life_and_government.regional_profile:
Puttaswamy's most direct dealings with government run through two channels: the cooperative sugar mill and irrigation bureaucracy that decide his income, and the panchayat and revenue offices that administer welfare schemes and land records. When cane payments run late, as they have in multiple recent crushing seasons, district administrations have had to formally order sugar factories to release pending price and subsidy amounts owed to farmers, splitting a top-up payment between the state government's share and a matching contribution from the mills themselves. Puttaswamy has joined roadside protests outside mill gates organised loosely under the banner of the Karnataka Rajya Raitha Sangha, the farmers' organisation with a strong base in Mandya, when a season's arrears stretch past what the household can absorb.

The other recurring flashpoint is water. In deficient-monsoon years, when the Cauvery Water Management Authority orders Karnataka to release water from the KRS reservoir to Tamil Nadu, farmers in Mandya have mounted sustained protests at Sanjay Circle and blocked the old Bengaluru-Mysuru highway; in one such standoff in August 2023, Karnataka initially offered to release 3,000 cusecs against a Tamil Nadu demand for 12,500 cusecs before the two sides settled on an interim release of 5,000 cusecs for fifteen days. Puttaswamy has taken part in these protests when they coincide with a season in which his own canal turn has already been cut short, experiencing the dispute as a direct threat to his second paddy crop rather than an abstract inter-state issue.

On welfare delivery, his household holds a Priority Household ration card under the state's Anna Bhagya scheme, entitling the family to a fixed quantity of free foodgrain each month on top of the earlier subsidised PDS allocation, and he has used MGNREGA job-card work on village road and canal-desilting projects in at least two lean seasons to cover a cash shortfall between crops. Land records for his holding are registered under the state's Bhoomi digitisation system, which he trusts more than he trusts the mill's payment ledger, though he has twice had to visit the taluk revenue office to correct a survey-number discrepancy affecting his share of the family's divided land. He has never contested a panchayat election himself but votes in every gram panchayat, assembly and parliamentary election, and follows Mandya's Lok Sabha and assembly results closely because, in his view, whichever party controls the state decides how fast cane arrears get paid.

worldview_and_concerns.definition: What this person worries about, is proud of, blames and demands, and how they would frame a public problem such as school dropout, drought, healthcare access or unemployment.
worldview_and_concerns.regional_profile:
Puttaswamy takes evident pride in Mandya's identity as the Cauvery-irrigated sugar bowl of Karnataka, and in the legacy of the KRS dam and the Mysore-era engineer Visvesvaraya, whose modernisation projects he regards as the foundation of the irrigation system his family still depends on. At the same time, he shares a grievance documented as widespread across Mandya, Ramanagara and Chamarajanagara: a sense that the state government, however proud of Mysuru's heritage or Bengaluru's technology economy, treats agrarian distress in districts like his as secondary to the capital's priorities, a perception that persists in regional accounts even though the state's most recent chief ministers have themselves come from the region.

Asked to explain why children in villages like his sometimes leave school before finishing the tenth standard, Puttaswamy would not frame it as a failure of will on the part of families. Based on his own reasoning about Kiran's situation, he would point instead to the collision between the cane and paddy calendar and the school calendar, the cost and safety of travelling beyond the village once a child reaches PU college age, and the fact that a household already waiting on a delayed mill payment cannot easily absorb the cost of transport, books or uniforms for a second child at once; this is an inference drawn from his own household's decisions rather than a claim he has stated in exactly these words.

On water, he draws a sharp line between two disputes that outsiders sometimes conflate: the decades-old Cauvery-sharing dispute with Tamil Nadu, which he experiences directly whenever a release order cuts his canal turn, and the newer, still-unresolved Mekedatu reservoir proposal on the same river, which he supports because he understands it as a way to store more of Karnataka's own share of Cauvery water rather than release it downstream, even though he is aware Tamil Nadu and some environmental groups oppose it for different reasons. He blames the Cauvery Water Management Authority's release orders and, more diffusely, Tamil Nadu's court petitions, for the years his second paddy crop fails, while reserving a separate and more personal frustration for the sugar mills, whom he blames directly for payment delays regardless of which government is in power.

On healthcare, his frustration is less about disputes and more about distance: anything beyond a fever or minor injury means a trip to Mandya town or, for serious conditions, to Mysuru, and a day spent travelling for treatment is a day of lost farm labour the household can rarely spare. On his children's future, he wants Chaitra to finish PU college and, if possible, a diploma or degree that could lead to a government job or a position in a Bengaluru-based company, and wants Kiran to inherit the farm eventually but only after finishing secondary school, a sequencing he insists on more firmly since watching neighbours' sons abandon school permanently for cane-cutting wages. He is proud of being a farmer but does not want either of his children to depend on farming alone, a view he attributes to the unpredictability of both weather and mill payments rather than to any dissatisfaction with agrarian life itself.
